timedelta(days=7) train = transactions[transactions.t_dat < cutoff] val = transactions[transactions.t_dat >= cutoff] # Generate validation ground truth val_gt = val.groupby("customer_id").article_id.apply(list).reset_index() val_gt.columns = ["customer_id", "actual"] # Train recommendation model customer_articles = ( train.groupby(["customer_id", "article_id"]) .agg(count=("article_id", "size"), last_date=("t_dat", "max")) .reset_index() .sort_values(["customer_id", "count", "last_date"], ascending=[True, False, False]) ) # Get top articles per customer top_articles = ( customer_articles.groupby("customer_id") .head(12) .groupby("customer_id") .article_id.apply(list) .reset_index() ) # Get popular items fallback popular = train.article_id.value_counts().head(12).index.tolist() # Generate validation predictions val_preds = pd.DataFrame(val_gt["customer_id"]).merge( top_articles, on="customer_id", how="left" ) val_preds["article_id"] = val_preds.article_id.apply( lambda x: x if isinstance(x, list) else [] ) def fill_preds(articles): needed = 12 - len(articles) return articles + popular[:needed] if needed > 0 else articles[:12] val_preds["predicted"] = val_preds.article_id.apply(fill_preds) val_eval = val_preds.merge(val_gt, on="customer_id", how="left") # Calculate validation score (exclude customers with no purchases) val_eval["actual"] = val_eval.actual.apply(lambda x: x if isinstance(x, list) else []) val_eval = val_eval[val_eval.actual.map(len) > 0] map12 = mapk(val_eval.actual.tolist(), val_preds.predicted.tolist()) print(f"Validation MAP@12: {map12:.4f}") # Full model training customer_articles_full = ( transactions.groupby(["customer_id", "article_id"]) .agg(count=("article_id", "size"), last_date=("t_dat", "max")) .reset_index() .sort_values(["customer_id", "count", "last_date"], ascending=[True, False, False]) ) top_articles_full = ( customer_articles_full.groupby("customer_id") .head(12) .groupby("customer_id") .article_id.apply(list) .reset_index() ) popular_full = transactions.article_id.value_counts().head(12).index.tolist() # Generate final submission submission = pd.read_csv( "./input/sample_submission.csv", dtype={"customer_id": "string"} )[["customer_id"]] submission = submission.merge(top_articles_full, on="customer_id", how="left") submission["article_id"] = submission.article_id.apply( lambda x: x if isinstance(x, list) else [] ) submission["prediction"] = submission.article_id.apply(fill_preds).apply( lambda x: " ".join(str(a) for a in x[:12]) ) # Ensure proper submission format submission[["customer_id", "prediction"]].to_csv( "./submission/submission.csv", index=False )

To address this recommendation task, we'll use a two-step approach: candidate
generation followed by LightGBM ranking. First, generate per-user candidates
using their top recent purchases and popular items, then train a model on user-
article features to rank these candidates. The model will be validated on a
time-based split to compute MAP@12, then applied to all users for submission.

The error occurs because `user_last_purchases` is a Series where groupby is
being called on the 'customer_id' index. The fix involves resetting the index
before grouping to properly access the customer_id column. Additionally, we need
to ensure all customer IDs from the sample submission are included in the final
predictions.

To address the H&M recommendation task, we'll use a hybrid approach combining
customers' historical purchases and global article popularity. We first generate
personalized recommendations based on each customer's most frequently and
recently purchased items. For customers with fewer than 12 items, we supplement
with the most popular articles overall. This balances personalization with cold-
start handling while maintaining computational efficiency.

The primary issue was merging a DataFrame with a Series instead of converting
the grouped Series to a DataFrame first. By resetting the index of the grouped
data, we ensure proper merging. Additionally, handling NaN values after merging
guarantees all customers get predictions filled with popular items.

To address the H&M recommendation challenge, we'll implement a recency and
popularity-based approach. This method prioritizes each customer's most recently
purchased items while filling gaps with globally popular articles. We'll split
transactions into a training and validation set based on time to evaluate
MAP@12. Finally, predictions for the test period are generated using the entire
dataset.

To address the timeout issue, we optimize the customer article lookup by using
dictionaries for O(1) access instead of DataFrame queries. This significantly
reduces processing time for the 1.3M customers. We also ensure proper handling
of missing customers by falling back to popular items.

The key issue is that using category dtype for article_id caused predictions to
store category codes instead of actual article_id strings. By converting these
columns to strings, we ensure correct IDs are used. Additionally, ensuring all
customers from the sample submission are included with proper merging and
filling missing predictions with popular items fixes submission generation.

The error occurs because validation predictions were incorrectly sliced,
resulting in NaN values. The fix involves ensuring all validation predictions
are properly filled with 12 articles and handling missing customer data
correctly. Additionally, the submission generation needs to ensure all customers
receive predictions even when no purchase history exists.

To address the H&M recommendation task, we'll leverage co-occurrence patterns of
articles purchased together. First, compute pairwise article co-occurrence
frequencies from transactions to identify items frequently bought in the same
session. For each customer, generate recommendations by aggregating top co-
occurring items from their most recent purchases. This captures collaborative
purchasing behavior while maintaining efficiency. Cold-start customers and gaps
in recommendations are filled using globally popular articles.
